title: The Afternoon Brief: Courts rule, floods crest, Iran escalates as Trump weighs oil over nukes
dek: A federal judge dismissed the administration's Harvard civil rights case on legal grounds, Midwest rivers hit multi-decade highs, and the administration publicly ranked low oil prices above nuclear containment in its Iran strategy as it prepared unprecedented sanctions.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The administration is explicitly prioritizing energy affordability over nuclear non-proliferation in Iran, signaling indefinite naval and economic pressure, while domestic crises, historic flooding, a high-profile murder case collision, and school violence, consume the news cycle.
bottom_line: Thursday's news cycle crystallized three competing priorities: the courts are narrowing civil rights enforcement thresholds, natural disaster is cresting at historic levels across the Midwest, and the administration is publicly reordering its Iran strategy to prioritize commodity prices over nuclear containment. Watch for Friday's Mangione plea hearing at 11 a.m., Treasury's sanctions announcement next week, state murder trial jury selection opening September 8, and whether the Strait of Hormuz dispute draws responses from other maritime powers or shipping insurers.
body: Three separate domains are reshaping the afternoon: the courts, the climate, and U.S. foreign strategy are each testing institutional capacity and political priority in ways that will unfold over weeks and months.

On civil rights enforcement, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns dismissed the Trump administration's Title VI lawsuit against Harvard on Thursday, finding that alleged antisemitic incidents in 2023-2024 and a handful in March 2025 were "too isolated and episodic" to meet the legal threshold for institutional noncompliance with federal civil rights law. The administration had alleged Harvard tolerated discrimination and sought to recover billions in federal subsidies. The ruling does not address the underlying incidents themselves, but rather whether they constitute an ongoing pattern. The DOJ indicated it will assess next steps; the Civil Rights Division's ongoing administrative investigation may pursue remedies outside the courts.

Flood conditions across Indiana and the Midwest reached a fourth consecutive day of crisis Thursday. The White River at Muncie was cresting at its highest level in more than 80 years, with forecasters projecting it will crest downstream at Anderson at its highest in more than 100 years by Thursday evening. Parts of eastern Indiana have taken 6 to nearly 12 inches of rain this week. More than 250,000 Indiana customers were without power Thursday morning, and two deaths have been reported in the state. At least four rivers are forecast to reach major flood stage into Thursday, meaning flooding can persist after the heaviest rain has stopped.

The Mangione murder case faces a legal collision Friday. Luigi Mangione is expected to plead guilty in federal court Friday at 11 a.m. to charges related to the December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson. A federal guilty plea could bar or derail the separate state murder prosecution under New York law, a consequence the Manhattan District Attorney has warned the federal court about in writing. State jury selection begins September 8. The outcome of Friday's federal hearing will determine whether New York's double-jeopardy rules operate to block state prosecution.

The Trump administration disclosed a structural vulnerability in its tariff strategy Thursday: it estimates losing $19 billion to $26 billion annually in tariff revenue as goods, primarily from China, are rerouted through more than 40 countries including Mexico and Malaysia to evade duties. This transshipping practice allows goods to enter at lower tariff rates or avoid them altogether. The administration has disclosed the problem but has not yet proposed enforcement mechanisms.

On Iran, Vice President JD Vance stated Thursday that keeping oil and gas prices low is the United States' "goal number one" in the Iran war, ranked explicitly above preventing Iran's nuclear program, designated "goal number two." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the naval blockade can continue "indefinitely." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessant announced that unprecedented economic sanctions are coming next week. The administration has also disputed Iran's assertion of control over the Strait of Hormuz, with Trump writing on Truth Social that the U.S. has "total control." Iran's Basij paramilitary chief countered that the Strait is "under Iran's control and management."

In other violence, a 17-year-old in Massachusetts has been charged with murdering his mother and 14-year-old brother after using ChatGPT to search for ideas about killing family members, according to prosecutors. In Georgia, a 14-year-old student allegedly shot another student in a Warner Robins High School bathroom during an argument Wednesday afternoon; one student was injured. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt announced Thursday she will leave her post at the end of August. In Japan, record rainfall killed at least eight people and displaced thousands, with Chiba prefecture recording the highest rainfall ever documented in Japan, nearly three times the average August monthly total.

An NYPD officer, Omar Habib, was convicted Thursday under New York City's 2020 chokehold ban for the first time, found guilty of second-degree felony strangulation, third-degree misdemeanor assault, and violating the city's ban enacted after George Floyd's death. He faces up to seven years in prison and has been terminated from the department.

Ukraine struck Russia's Novorossiysk port on the Black Sea with a massive drone and missile barrage, damaging two major grain export terminals and hitting Russia's last significant naval base on the Black Sea. Three people, including an eight-year-old child, were killed and 24 injured. Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter; August shipments could fall more than half due to the disruption.
